entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cao Pi (187–226 CE), the eldest surviving son of the powerful warlord Cao Cao, founded the state of Cao Wei and became its first emperor, Emperor Wen, in 220 CE. His usurpation of Emperor Xian of Han formally ended the Eastern Han Dynasty, initiating the Three Kingdoms period (220–280 CE) in China, a pivotal era of fragmentation, military innovation, and cultural flourishing. His reign established critical administrative and legal precedents for subsequent Chinese dynasties, fundamentally reshaping the political landscape of East Asia for centuries.

After Cao Cao's death in 220 CE, Cao Pi inherited his father's title of King of Wei and the chancellorship. Within months, he compelled Emperor Xian to abdicate, thereby ending the Han Dynasty's 400-year rule and proclaiming himself emperor of Wei, based in Luoyang. During his six-year reign, Cao Pi introduced the Nine-rank system (九品官人法) for official appointments, a meritocratic (though often abused) method intended to select talent for bureaucracy. He also engaged in military campaigns against the rival states of Shu Han and Eastern Wu, though largely without decisive success, consolidating Wei's northern borders. As a prominent poet and literary critic, he was a leading figure in the Jian'an literary style, known for his work like the "Discourse on Literature" (典論·論文).
